question: What is Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)?
answer:
SSRF is a vulnerability where an attacker convinces a server to make HTTP (or other) requests to URLs of the attacker's choosing, leveraging the server's network position and trust relationships.

Classic example: an image-resizing endpoint takes a URL parameter (?url=https://example.com/cat.jpg) and the server fetches it. An attacker submits ?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ — the IP for AWS EC2 instance metadata. The server, running on EC2 with no firewall rules between it and metadata, fetches that URL and returns AWS credentials in the response.

What makes SSRF dangerous:
- The server can usually reach internal addresses you cannot (RFC1918 ranges, internal services, cloud metadata).
- The server's identity (IAM role, internal mTLS cert, allowed source IP) authorizes it to call services your attacker couldn't.
- The protocol may be anything the server's HTTP library supports — http, https, ftp, file:, gopher: — each opening new attack surface.

SSRF in OWASP A10:2021. It's promoted up the list every year because the cloud era made it especially devastating.

question: What are common SSRF entry points in a web app?
answer:
Any feature where the server makes an outbound request based on user input:

1. URL preview / link unfurl: paste a URL into chat / a comment; the server fetches it to show a preview.
2. Image / file fetchers: "import from URL," avatar upload by URL, image resizing services.
3. PDF / screenshot generation: "render this URL as PDF" — headless browser fetches the URL.
4. Webhooks: user-configured outbound notifications. The user gets to choose the URL.
5. SSO / OIDC discovery: server fetches /.well-known/openid-configuration from a user-supplied issuer URL.
6. RSS / feed importers: user submits a feed URL; server fetches and parses.
7. XML/SOAP processors: XXE-style attacks turn into SSRF when external entities are resolved.
8. SVG renderers: SVGs can include xlink:href to external resources.
9. Embedded URL validators: a tool that fetches a URL to check if it's reachable / valid.
10. Email clients: image proxying for tracking pixel privacy can become SSRF.
11. Document parsers (Office, PDF): cross-references that fetch over the network.
12. Health check endpoints: ?target=http://x — admin probes that take URL parameters.
13. OAuth callback / redirect handling: server-side redirect logic that follows attacker-controlled URLs.

The common thread: server-side network egress with attacker-controlled destinations.

question: Why is blocklist-based SSRF defense ("reject URLs containing 169.254.169.254") inadequate?
answer:
Attackers have many ways to express the same destination address; a blocklist must enumerate them all and inevitably misses some:

1. Decimal IP: http://2852039166 == http://169.254.169.254.
2. Octal: http://0251.0376.0251.0376 == 169.254.169.254.
3. Hex: http://0xA9FEA9FE == 169.254.169.254.
4. Zero-prefix: http://0/ == 0.0.0.0 == localhost on many stacks.
5. IPv6 mapping: http://[::ffff:169.254.169.254].
6. IPv6 link-local with zone: http://[fe80::1%eth0].
7. URL-encoded: http://169%2e254%2e169%2e254.
8. Username/password injection: http://www.google.com@169.254.169.254/ — many parsers extract the host as the legitimate one but fetch the attacker's.
9. DNS rebinding: a domain that resolves to a public IP on first lookup and 169.254.169.254 on second. The blocklist sees the public IP; the actual fetch hits metadata.
10. Redirects: a public URL the server fetches returns a 302 to the metadata endpoint.
11. Alternate metadata IPs: GCP uses metadata.google.internal -> 169.254.169.254 with a Host header check; Azure has its own; new clouds have new endpoints — keeping a blocklist current is endless.
12. SSRF via different protocols: gopher://, dict://, ftp:// to internal services.

A blocklist is also fragile against renamed internal services (a new microservice with a previously-unblocked DNS name); the universe of dangerous destinations grows faster than the list.

The right approach is an allowlist (explicit list of acceptable outbound destinations) AND post-resolution validation (after DNS resolves the hostname, confirm the resulting IP is in an allowed range BEFORE connecting). Plus network-level controls: block the metadata IP at the egress firewall, give different IAM roles to different services, use IMDSv2 (which requires a session token and blocks SSRF-style metadata theft on AWS).

question: What is DNS rebinding and how does it relate to SSRF?
answer:
DNS rebinding is an attack where the attacker controls a domain whose DNS records change between successive lookups, exploiting a Time-Of-Check-To-Time-Of-Use gap in the client.

Attack flow against a server-side fetcher:
1. Attacker controls evil.example.
2. Server validates the URL https://evil.example/path: resolves evil.example, gets 203.0.113.42 (public IP), checks against allowlist, passes.
3. Server initiates the HTTP request. Many HTTP clients re-resolve the hostname between connection attempts, or use a connection pool that re-resolves periodically.
4. Second DNS lookup for evil.example returns 169.254.169.254 (metadata IP) because the attacker's DNS server has a very short TTL and rebound the name.
5. Server connects to 169.254.169.254 carrying the original Host: evil.example header. AWS metadata responds to whatever IP a request arrived at (in IMDSv1) — credentials are returned.

Defenses:
- Resolve the hostname once, then connect directly to the resulting IP, passing the original hostname in a SNI/Host header. The server controls the IP it connects to.
- Validate the resolved IP against an allowlist BEFORE connecting.
- Reuse the same resolved address for the lifetime of the request and pin it.
- Use a hardened HTTP client library that handles SSRF-safe resolution (e.g., url-parse + manual socket with explicit IP).
- Network-level: block egress to RFC1918 / link-local from app servers entirely; let the app speak only to a controlled proxy that validates destinations.
- AWS specifically: enable IMDSv2 (token-based, requires PUT + custom header). Defeats DNS rebinding against metadata because the unrelated PUT request is what gets the token, and the server has to add a header an attacker can't.

DNS rebinding bypasses naive URL validators because the validator and the actual fetcher disagree about where the URL points.

question: Design SSRF defense in depth for a service that legitimately needs to fetch user-supplied URLs (e.g., webhook delivery).
answer:
Treat outbound network access as a privileged operation that needs explicit policy.

Layer 1 — URL validation (per request):
1. Parse the URL with a robust parser; reject if parsing is ambiguous.
2. Allowed schemes: https only (block http, ftp, file, gopher, data, etc.).
3. Block obvious traps: userinfo (user@host), unusual ports, URL-encoded host characters.
4. Resolve the hostname yourself. Check ALL resolved IPs against a deny-list of internal ranges (RFC1918, link-local 169.254.0.0/16, loopback 127.0.0.0/8, IPv6 equivalents, metadata IPs, your own VPC CIDRs).
5. If the deny-list check passes, connect to a SPECIFIC IP (not the hostname again). Pin the IP for the lifetime of the request to defeat DNS rebinding.
6. Set a strict Host header to the original hostname.

Layer 2 — HTTP behavior:
7. No redirect following, or follow with re-validation at every hop. A 302 to internal_service is the most common rebinding bypass.
8. Tight timeouts (connect + read) so slow responses can't be used for timing oracles.
9. Strict response size caps (e.g., 5MB). Avoid streaming attacks.
10. Content-Type allowlist if applicable (image fetchers should reject text/html).

Layer 3 — Network isolation:
11. Egress proxy: outbound HTTP from the app service goes through a dedicated proxy host that enforces destination policy independently. The app can't directly reach internal IPs even if its code is buggy.
12. NACLs / security groups: app servers have egress rules that deny RFC1918 and metadata IPs by default. Only the proxy is permitted broader egress.
13. Separate VPC subnet for outbound-heavy services so a compromised one can't pivot to internal infra.

Layer 4 — Identity hardening:
14. AWS: enforce IMDSv2 cluster-wide. Disable IMDSv1 entirely. Token-bound metadata defeats SSRF-as-credential-theft.
15. GCP: set metadata-flavor headers / disable legacy metadata.
16. Use scoped IAM roles. The webhook-sender service has permissions ONLY for what webhook-sending needs — not S3 admin, not RDS, not anything else. SSRF gives the attacker the role's powers; minimize them.

Layer 5 — Monitoring:
17. Log every outbound URL and resolved IP. Anomaly-detect on internal IPs ever appearing as fetch targets (should be 0).
18. Alert on first-time external destinations from each service ("webhook-sender just fetched a previously-unseen domain — is that expected?").
19. Track DNS resolution patterns. Sudden bursts of short-TTL lookups from one service may flag rebinding attempts.

Layer 6 — Operational:
20. Webhook target verification before saving the URL: have the customer prove ownership of the target by responding to a challenge. Disincentivizes attackers using your platform for stealth attacks against third parties.
21. Customer-side egress: where feasible, push outbound delivery to the customer's network instead of yours ("pull" not "push" semantics).
22. Tested incident playbook: if SSRF is exploited, who rotates which credentials in what order?

The meta-rule: a defense that depends only on URL validation will eventually fail. Defense in depth so that network + identity + monitoring catches the leak when validation fails.

question: Why is SSRF particularly damaging in cloud environments, and how does IMDSv2 help?
answer:
Cloud environments couple compute identity with reachable metadata services accessible from anywhere on the host:

1. Metadata service identity: in AWS, every EC2 instance can ask 169.254.169.254 "what IAM role am I?" — and the metadata service returns temporary STS credentials with whatever permissions the instance role has. No authentication needed beyond "running on this instance."

2. Internal-only addressability: 169.254.169.254 isn't routable from the internet — it's host-local. This makes the metadata service inherently trustworthy IF you assume only your own code talks to it. SSRF breaks that assumption: now an external attacker is effectively running code that asks for credentials.

3. Lateral movement: stolen IAM credentials let the attacker pivot across the cloud account. STS, S3, RDS, internal VPC services, secrets manager — all accept the credential. SSRF -> full cloud account takeover is a documented path (Capital One, 2019).

4. Network position privileges: services running inside a VPC may reach databases, internal APIs, and microservices that lack any authentication beyond "if you can reach me, you're trusted." SSRF lets an external attacker speak from this trusted position.

IMDSv2 (Instance Metadata Service v2) mitigates many SSRF-against-metadata attacks:

Mechanism: instead of a single GET, IMDSv2 requires:
1. A PUT request to /latest/api/token with a custom header X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600 to obtain a session token.
2. Subsequent GETs include X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: <token>.

Why this helps:
- PUT method: most SSRF gadgets only support GET. The attacker can't trivially perform the PUT to get a token.
- Custom header: most SSRF gadgets don't allow arbitrary header injection. Even if the attacker can issue PUT, they can't add the required header.
- TTL on the token: tokens default to short TTLs; can be tuned by hop limit (so containerized workloads can't even relay tokens).
- IP hop limit: tokens won't traverse beyond N IP hops (configurable to 1) — preventing token re-use from sidecar containers.

IMDSv2 doesn't make SSRF safe; it makes the metadata-credential-theft pattern much harder. An attacker with a fully-featured SSRF (arbitrary methods, arbitrary headers) can still reach IMDSv2 — but the bar is much higher than IMDSv1's single GET. Enforce IMDSv2-only mode at the account level (no fallback to IMDSv1). It's the single highest-impact knob you can turn for cloud SSRF hardening.

Analogous mechanisms exist on GCP (metadata-flavor header required) and Azure (similar). The general principle: metadata services should never be reachable by accident from anyone less trusted than the code running on the host.
